additions.title: Temporal quality degradation in AI models
additions.publisher: Scientific Reports (Nature Portfolio); authors Daniel Vela, Andrew Sharp, Richard Zhang, Trang Nguyen, An Hoang and Oleg S. Pianykh
additions.quote: we observed temporal model degradation in 91% of cases
additions.why: Peer-reviewed, open-access evidence for why risk has to be looked at again after go-live: across 128 pairings of four standard model types with 32 datasets from healthcare operations, transport, finance and weather, quality fell with time since training in 91%. The nearest thing found to a defensible figure for this criterion. Limits: time-series prediction models, not language models; not UK data; the datasets were chosen by the authors, so the percentage describes their sample, not all AI systems.

additions.title: How is ChatGPT's behavior changing over time?
additions.publisher: arXiv (authors' copy; later published in Harvard Data Science Review); authors Lingjiao Chen, Matei Zaharia, James Zou
additions.quote: when and how these models are updated over time is opaque
additions.why: Evidence that a bought-in AI service can change without the customer being told: the same two services, tested in March and June 2023, gave markedly different results on the same tasks, better on some and worse on others. Supports a review trigger for supplier model changes and the authors' call for continuous monitoring. Limits: two products from one supplier over three months; the arXiv copy is cited because the journal's own page refused automated access; findings are dated.

additions.title: FCA Handbook, PRIN 2A.9: Monitoring of consumer outcomes
additions.quote: A firm must regularly monitor the outcomes retail customers receive from
additions.why: A binding UK rule requiring continuing monitoring of results, not of documents: firms must regularly monitor the outcomes customers receive, be able to tell whether any group is getting worse outcomes than another, find root causes and act. It applies however the outcome is produced, so it covers AI used in retail financial services. Limits: FCA-authorised firms serving retail customers only; not AI-specific; frequency is left to the firm.

additions.title: The Medical Devices (Post-market Surveillance Requirements) (Amendment) (Great Britain) Regulations 2024, regulation 4 (new Part 4A)
additions.locator: Regulation 4, inserted regulation 44ZE(1) to (4); regulation 44ZF (surveillance plan)
additions.quote: includes the analysis of data relevant to the quality, performance and safety of the device throughout its lifetime
additions.why: UK legislation that makes lifecycle monitoring a legal duty for one class of AI: a manufacturer must keep a post-market surveillance system for each device, proportionate to its risk, covering its whole lifetime, and use the data to update its risk analysis and to spot trends in incidents. Limits: manufacturers of medical devices only, not users; Great Britain; the as-made text; later amendments not checked.

additions.title: Code of Practice for the Cyber Security of AI
additions.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
additions.locator: Principle 12 'Monitor your system’s behaviour', provisions 12.2 and 12.4
additions.quote: monitor the performance of their models and system over time so that they can detect sudden or gradual changes in behaviour
additions.why: The UK government code's monitoring principle, addressed to organisations that deploy AI as well as those that build it: analyse logs to confirm the system still produces the desired outputs and to detect drift or unexpected behaviour, and watch performance over time. Limits: voluntary; written for security, so it frames change in behaviour as a security concern.

additions.title: Artificial Intelligence Playbook for the UK Government
additions.locator: Principle 5: 'You understand how to manage the full AI life cycle'
additions.quote: You should understand how to monitor and mitigate for potential drift, bias, and, in the case of generative AI, hallucinations.
additions.why: Current UK government guidance to its own departments: an AI system has a full life cycle to manage, with a robust testing and monitoring process in place to catch drift and bias, and a plan for updating the system and closing it down. Limits: guidance for the public sector, not binding on companies; principles, not a monitoring method.

additions.title: AI tools in recruitment: audit outcomes report
additions.locator: Section 'Accuracy, fairness, and bias mitigation in AI', findings on accuracy testing
additions.quote: The majority of AI providers repeated accuracy tests at least periodically after launch and especially before implementing changes or updates.
additions.why: What the UK regulator found when it audited real AI suppliers: most retested accuracy after launch and before changes so that it 'did not erode over time', but its example is a provider that had not formally assessed accuracy before launch. The regulator assessed whether providers 'regularly monitored accuracy and bias' through the lifecycle. Limits: consensual audits of recruitment-tool developers and providers between August 2023 and May 2024; a snapshot; gives no counts.

rejected.title: Ensuring statistical models command public confidence (review of the 2020 exam grading algorithms)
rejected.reason: Landing page read. Its lessons concern building public confidence during model development, not reassessment after deployment. Not relevant enough to this criterion.

rejected.title: R (Bridges) v Chief Constable of South Wales Police [2020] EWCA Civ 1058
rejected.reason: Considered and not fetched: the equality-duty finding concerns checks before and during a trial deployment and belongs with impact assessment and fairness criteria.

rejected.title: FG22/5: Final non-Handbook Guidance for firms on the Consumer Duty
rejected.reason: Served and opened; the binding handbook text (PRIN 2A.9) was preferred as the right kind of evidence for a duty.

brief_check: Nothing read contradicts the approved brief. It dates one line: the brief says 'No defensible figure was found'; a peer-reviewed study read today (Vela and others, Scientific Reports 2022, Results) reports model quality degrading over time in 91% of 128 model-and-dataset pairs. Whether that is defensible enough for a board paper is a judgement for the lead: it is not UK data and covers prediction models, not language models.
